varieties.name: Early Wonder Tall Top
varieties.notes: Quick, adaptable red beet with lush tops for greens; a good first sowing where springs are short.

varieties.name: Detroit Dark Red
varieties.notes: The classic all-purpose red beet; smooth, deep-red roots for fresh eating, canning and storage.

varieties.name: Red Ace
varieties.notes: Vigorous hybrid with even germination and sweet, uniform roots; reliable when conditions are less than ideal.

varieties.name: Chioggia
varieties.notes: Italian heirloom with red-and-white bullseye rings inside; mild and sweet, best roasted or raw.

varieties.name: Touchstone Gold
varieties.notes: Golden beet with better germination than older yellows; mild flavor and doesn't bleed onto other foods.

varieties.name: Bull's Blood
varieties.notes: Grown mainly for its glossy deep-burgundy leaves, great in salads; roots are usable when young.

varieties.name: Cylindra
varieties.notes: Long, carrot-shaped red roots give uniform slices and more yield per foot of row; good for canning.

varieties.name: Lutz Green Leaf
varieties.notes: Large late beet that stays tender at big sizes and keeps for months; sow for a fall storage crop.

varieties.name: Green Magic
varieties.notes: Heat-tolerant hybrid with smooth, domed heads; a top choice for spring crops that mature into warm weather.

varieties.name: Imperial
varieties.notes: Bred to head well in heat; a strong pick for late-spring and summer plantings in warm climates.

varieties.name: Belstar
varieties.notes: Widely adaptable hybrid with tight blue-green heads and good side shoots; works in spring and fall.

varieties.name: Marathon
varieties.notes: Very cold-tolerant hybrid for fall and overwintered crops; heads well in cool weather, poor in summer heat.

varieties.name: Waltham 29
varieties.notes: Old cold-tolerant standard for fall harvests; big blue-green heads plus side shoots. Not for hot weather.

varieties.name: Calabrese
varieties.notes: Italian heirloom with a medium central head followed by many side shoots over a long season.

varieties.name: De Cicco
varieties.notes: Fast Italian heirloom with small heads and abundant side shoots; good where the cool season is short.

varieties.name: Long Island Improved
varieties.notes: Classic compact heirloom; dependable for home gardens where falls are long and cool.

varieties.name: Jade Cross
varieties.notes: AAS-winning hybrid with more heat tolerance than heirlooms; a better bet where autumns stay warm.

varieties.name: Gladius
varieties.notes: Early, uniform sprouts that hold well on the stalk; sturdy plants resist toppling.

varieties.name: Dagan
varieties.notes: Productive hybrid with smooth, dark-green sprouts; a reliable main-season fall crop.

varieties.name: Silvia
varieties.notes: Tall, high-yielding hybrid with sweet, well-spaced sprouts that are easy to pick.

varieties.name: Divino
varieties.notes: Late-season hybrid for sweet sprouts picked after frost; best where falls are long and cold.

varieties.name: Golden Acre
varieties.notes: Early round-headed cabbage on compact plants; matures before summer heat or in short seasons.

varieties.name: Early Jersey Wakefield
varieties.notes: Early heirloom with small cone-shaped heads; tender and sweet, and fairly resistant to splitting.

varieties.name: Charleston Wakefield
varieties.notes: Larger, more heat-tolerant cousin of Jersey Wakefield; a long-time favorite in the South.

varieties.name: Copenhagen Market
varieties.notes: Danish heirloom with round, solid 3–4 lb heads; a dependable early-to-mid season kraut cabbage.

varieties.name: Red Express
varieties.notes: Fast, compact red cabbage with small solid heads; good where seasons are short or space is tight.

varieties.name: Alcosa
varieties.notes: Small, early savoy with crinkled, tender leaves; manageable size for home gardens.

varieties.name: Deadon
varieties.notes: January King-type with red-purple outer leaves; very frost hardy, sweetens in cold for late fall harvest.

varieties.name: Danish Ballhead
varieties.notes: Hardy late heirloom with dense heads that keep for months in cold storage; plant for fall harvest.

varieties.name: Snow Crown
varieties.notes: Fast, forgiving hybrid; one of the easiest cauliflowers for beginners and short cool seasons.

varieties.name: Twister
varieties.notes: Heat-tolerant white cauliflower with well-wrapped heads; a better choice where spring warms quickly.

varieties.name: Amazing
varieties.notes: Open-pollinated white with dense heads and leaves that curl over to self-blanch; spring or fall.

varieties.name: Snowball Y Improved
varieties.notes: Classic home-garden white; needs leaves tied over heads to keep curds white. Best as a fall crop.

varieties.name: Cheddar
varieties.notes: Bright orange heads high in beta-carotene; color deepens in sun and holds when cooked. No blanching needed.

varieties.name: Graffiti
varieties.notes: Vivid purple heads that need no blanching; color fades to blue-green if boiled, so roast or steam.

varieties.name: Veronica
varieties.notes: Romanesco with lime-green spiraled points; needs a long, steady cool season and even water.

varieties.name: Tango
varieties.notes: Uniform, tender green celery that is easier than most; a good pick for first-time growers.

varieties.name: Tall Utah 52-70R Improved
varieties.notes: Standard tall green celery with thick, crisp stalks; widely sold and dependable with steady water.

varieties.name: Merengo
varieties.notes: Vigorous hybrid with smooth, dark-green stalks; sow for a fall harvest if cool spring nights cause bolting.

varieties.name: Kelvin
varieties.notes: Tall hybrid with heavy, uniform, dark-green stalks and good flavor; a productive main-season choice.

varieties.name: Fordhook Giant
varieties.notes: Big, savoyed leaves on thick white stems; yields through hot summers and into fall.

varieties.name: Bright Lights
varieties.notes: Mix of red, yellow, orange, pink and white stems; as ornamental as it is productive.

varieties.name: Ruby Red
varieties.notes: Also sold as Rhubarb chard; crimson stalks and dark leaves. Can bolt if young plants get a cold snap.

varieties.name: Peppermint
varieties.notes: Pink-and-white striped stems on glossy leaves; great as baby leaf or full-size bunches.

varieties.name: Five Color Silverbeet
varieties.notes: Australian heirloom with mixed-color stems and mild leaves; a good alternative to Bright Lights.

varieties.name: Perpetual Spinach
varieties.notes: Thin-stemmed leaf chard that tastes like spinach and resists bolting; a summer spinach substitute in heat.

varieties.name: Georgia Southern
varieties.notes: Classic Southern collard tolerant of both heat and frost; a long-season choice in warm climates.

varieties.name: Vates
varieties.notes: Compact, slow-bolting Virginia heirloom; very cold hardy for fall and winter harvests.

varieties.name: Champion
varieties.notes: Improved Vates type with compact plants and a longer harvest before bolting; good in cold areas.

varieties.name: Flash
varieties.notes: Vigorous, uniform hybrid with smooth dark leaves; slow to bolt, so it extends spring harvests.

varieties.name: Top Bunch 2.0
varieties.notes: Fast hybrid with tender, slightly savoyed leaves; quick to first harvest from direct sowing.

varieties.name: Broad Windsor
varieties.notes: The standard fava, with big flat beans in 6–8 inch pods; sow very early in spring or in fall where mild.

varieties.name: Aquadulce Claudia
varieties.notes: The classic fall-sown fava; overwinters where winters are mild for an early spring crop.

varieties.name: Vroma
varieties.notes: Productive, relatively early fava with long pods; a good spring-sown choice where summers turn hot fast.

varieties.name: Extra Precoce a Grano Violetto
varieties.notes: Italian heirloom with purple beans; early, frost-tolerant, for early spring or fall sowing.

varieties.name: Early White Vienna
varieties.notes: Classic pale-green heirloom; crisp and mild when picked at 2–3 inches.

varieties.name: Purple Vienna
varieties.notes: Purple-skinned heirloom with white flesh; slightly hardier than white types, good for fall.

varieties.name: Konan
varieties.notes: Fast, uniform hybrid with smooth round bulbs that stay tender; good for quick spring crops.

varieties.name: Kolibri
varieties.notes: Quick purple hybrid with crisp, sweet white flesh; stays tender a bit longer than heirlooms.

varieties.name: Azur Star
varieties.notes: Early, flattened blue-purple bulbs; a good open-pollinated choice for early spring sowing.

varieties.name: Kossak
varieties.notes: Giant fall kohlrabi up to 8 inches that stays tender, not woody; stores for months in the cold.

varieties.name: King Richard
varieties.notes: Fast, long-shanked summer leek; good where seasons are short but not frost hardy, so harvest by late fall.

varieties.name: Megaton
varieties.notes: High-yielding hybrid with very long, thick shanks; holds well in the garden into fall.

varieties.name: Tadorna
varieties.notes: Blue-green fall leek that stands well in cold weather; a solid choice for late-fall harvests.

varieties.name: Giant Musselburgh
varieties.notes: Scottish heirloom with thick shanks; one of the hardiest leeks for overwintering in the ground.

varieties.name: Oslo
varieties.notes: Late hybrid bred for overwintering; stout plants hold through cold for winter and early spring harvest.

varieties.name: Bandit
varieties.notes: Very hardy overwintering leek with thick shanks and dark blue-green leaves; harvest winter to spring.

varieties.name: Red Giant
varieties.notes: Purple-tinged broad leaves with a hot bite; very slow to bolt and cold hardy enough to overwinter in mild areas.

varieties.name: Southern Giant Curled
varieties.notes: Classic Southern frilly mustard; large, bright-green leaves tolerate heat better than most greens.

varieties.name: Green Wave
varieties.notes: Very spicy curled mustard that is slow to bolt; a good pick for late-spring sowings.

varieties.name: Florida Broadleaf
varieties.notes: Large, smooth, mild leaves for cooking greens; a Southern staple for fall and winter sowing.

varieties.name: Golden Frills
varieties.notes: Lacy chartreuse leaves with mild heat; tolerates both heat and cold, great as baby salad greens.

varieties.name: Ruby Streaks
varieties.notes: Finely cut purple-green leaves with mild spice; a colorful salad mustard for cool seasons.

varieties.name: Tendergreen
varieties.notes: Komatsuna-type 'mustard spinach' with mild, smooth leaves; grows fast and handles more heat than spinach.

varieties.name: Joi Choi
varieties.notes: Large, vigorous white-stem pac choi; slow to bolt and tolerant of cold, a reliable spring or fall pick.

varieties.name: Black Summer
varieties.notes: Dark-leaved, green-stemmed choi bred for summer; holds better in heat than most bok choy.

varieties.name: Bopak
varieties.notes: Tall, heavy, uniform white-stem heads with mild flavor; tolerates warm weather well.

varieties.name: Mei Qing Choi
varieties.notes: Compact Shanghai-type with pale green stems; a good medium-size choi for spring and fall.

varieties.name: Li Ren Choi
varieties.notes: Green-stem baby choi that fills out at small size; quick to harvest and good for close spacing.

varieties.name: Toy Choi
varieties.notes: Miniature white-stem choi ready in about a month; ideal for containers and quick crops before heat.

varieties.name: Arugula (Roquette)
varieties.notes: Standard salad arugula with nutty, peppery lobed leaves; very fast in cool weather, bolts in heat.

varieties.name: Astro
varieties.notes: Early, heat-tolerant arugula with milder, strap-shaped leaves; extends harvests into warm weather.

varieties.name: Esmee
varieties.notes: Oakleaf-shaped, ruffled leaves with mild flavor; good for overwintering under cover.

varieties.name: Sylvetta
varieties.notes: Wild arugula (Diplotaxis): slower-growing, deeply lobed, more pungent, slower to bolt; often perennial.

varieties.name: Bellezia
varieties.notes: Larger, more vigorous wild arugula with dark, serrated leaves; regrows well after cutting.

varieties.name: Hollow Crown
varieties.notes: Classic heirloom with long, smooth roots; needs deep, loose soil. Sweetens after frost.

varieties.name: All American
varieties.notes: Thick, wedge-shaped roots that size up a bit sooner; better for shorter seasons or heavier soil.

varieties.name: Harris Model
varieties.notes: Smooth, white heirloom-type roots with little side-rooting; leave in the ground through frost.

varieties.name: Javelin
varieties.notes: Slender, uniform hybrid with good canker resistance; easier to dig than giant types.

varieties.name: Gladiator
varieties.notes: Vigorous hybrid with quick early growth and smooth white roots; canker resistant.

varieties.name: Purple Top White Globe
varieties.notes: The classic purple-shouldered turnip; harvest small for sweetness or let size up for fall storage.

varieties.name: Hakurei
varieties.notes: Smooth white salad turnip, sweet enough to eat raw; tender tops are excellent too.

varieties.name: Tokyo Cross
varieties.notes: AAS-winning white turnip ready at 2 inches in about five weeks; good for quick spring or fall crops.

varieties.name: Scarlet Queen
varieties.notes: Red-skinned salad turnip with white flesh and red-stemmed greens; colorful and mild.

varieties.name: Golden Ball
varieties.notes: Also called Orange Jelly; yellow-fleshed heirloom with fine, sweet flavor that keeps well.

varieties.name: Seven Top
varieties.notes: Grown for leaves, not roots; hardy Southern turnip green that can be cut repeatedly through winter.

varieties.name: American Purple Top
varieties.notes: The standard rutabaga with purple shoulders and yellow flesh; sweetens with frost and stores well.

varieties.name: Laurentian
varieties.notes: Canadian-bred, uniform purple-top roots with mild yellow flesh; a reliable keeper.

varieties.name: Helenor
varieties.notes: Smooth, uniform roots with sweet orange-yellow flesh; good eating quality fresh or stored.

varieties.name: Joan
varieties.notes: Refined American Purple Top type with smooth, round roots and sweet, mild flesh that improves after frost.
